source_caption:
Dead Poets Society feels like a quiet kind of rebellion, built around youth, pressure, and the need to think for yourself.

Inside the strict world of Welton Academy, Mr. Keating, played by Robin Williams, doesn’t just teach poetry, he pushes his students to question things, to feel more, and to actually live. “Carpe Diem” isn’t just a line, it becomes something that slowly changes how they see their lives.

The film is soft but powerful at the same time, showing how words and ideas can shape who you become. It’s not really about school, it’s about finding your own voice, even when it comes with consequences. And yeah, it’s the kind of story that stays with you long after it ends.

source_details.title: Dead Poets Society
source_details.synopsis: Dead Poets Society is a 1989 American coming-of-age film directed by Peter Weir and written by Tom Schulman. It stars Robin Williams and is set in 1959 at a fictional boarding school called Welton Academy, and focuses around a select group of boys, who over time take several pieces of advice from their English teacher, John Keating (Williams). Schulman wrote the script for Dead Poets Society in 1985 based on his own experiences at the Montgomery Bell Academy in Nashville, Tennessee. Jeff Kanew was originally hired as director, but was eventually replaced by Weir. Weir met with Jeffrey Katzenberg, the CEO of Disney in 1988, who suggested Weir read Schulman's script.
